extracted.intended_audience: educated readers of political pamphlets, commentators, and policymakers (late-18th-century British public and political readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing political pamphlets and public-policy proposals for practical feasibility, consistency with existing institutions, financial realism, and likely consequences. Emphasizes logistical, constitutional, and economic considerations when judging reforms or speculative projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility of means
rubrics_metrics.description: Men of sense ... must see the means of compassing it to be next to certain; the mischiefs not to counterbalance the profit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a proposed project has practical, near-certain means of implementation rather than relying on theoretical rights or grand declarations. Question whether the mechanics and necessary resources actually exist to accomplish the plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearly stated and relevant ends
rubrics_metrics.description: As the author has stated this Indian taxation for no visible purpose relative to his plan of supply ... many other projects with as little, if any distinct end;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require each proposal to state a clear, specific purpose tied to the larger plan; avoid speculative policies that have no demonstrable relation to the supposed objective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial realism and accounting
rubrics_metrics.description: All that he bestows upon the nation ... amounts to no more than a sum of 300,000_l._ a year. So much for these revenues; which are nothing but his visions, or already the national possessions without any act of his.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that revenue estimates are real, not double-counted or already possessed; account for existing revenues, obligations, and how newly proposed taxes substitute or replace current ones. Distinguish imaginary revenue from existing funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't base national policy on single persons' continued power
rubrics_metrics.description: So we are staked on four chances; his power, its permanence, the success of his projects, and the duration of his life. Any one of these failing, we are gone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid policies that hinge on the continued life, influence, or unique capabilities of one individual. Assess risks if leadership changes or the individual fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and prudence for constitutional change
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience shows us, that no time can be fit for such changes but a time of general confusion ... Perhaps a time of the greatest security and tranquillity both at home and abroad may likewise be fit; but will the author affirm this to be just such a time?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the present political moment is appropriate for major constitutional alterations; avoid proposing sweeping reforms during crises or when public authority is unsettled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of habits, prejudices, and affected opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: They will examine how a proposed imposition or regulation agrees with the opinion of those who are likely to be affected by it; they will not despise the consideration even of their habitudes and prejudices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate compatibility of reforms with entrenched customs and public sentiment. Proposals should account for likely reception and the social/cultural friction they will face.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for differing institutional purposes (avoid Procrustean uniformity)
rubrics_metrics.description: An attempt towards a compulsory equality in all circumstances, and an exact practical definition of the supreme rights in every case, is the most dangerous and chimerical of all enterprises ... Procrustes shall never be my hero of legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid one-size-fits-all solutions that try to force different institutions into uniform roles; assess each institution according to its distinct function and history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of stirring controversy merely to balance discontent
rubrics_metrics.description: What I object to, is their introduction into a discourse relating to the immediate state of our affairs, and recommending plans of practical government ... an attempt to raise discontent in the people of England, to balance those discontents which the measures of his friends had already raised in America.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticize proposals that appear designed to manufacture political support rather than to solve problems. Assess authorial motive and whether proposals are sincere solutions or rhetorical balancing acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for logistical practicalities (esp. remote representation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The writs are issued ... Some provinces receive them in six weeks, some in ten, some in twenty ... The members are chosen; and if ships are ready to sail, in about six more they arrive in London ... the Parliament has sat and business far advanced without American representatives ... Does the author mean to make our kings as immortal ... or are the American representatives to be perpetual?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine transportation times, communication delays, re-election cycles, wartime risks, and other logistical realities when proposing representation for remote territories. Model how the mechanics will work in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic feasibility for representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Some of the most considerable provinces of America ... have not in each of them two men who can afford, at a distance from their estates, to spend a thousand pounds a year. How can these provinces be represented at Westminster?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether prospective representatives can afford to serve without undue dependence (e.g., salaries, patronage). Consider whether paying deputies would make them agents rather than independent legislators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency between declared principles and actions
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to excuse any appearance of inconsistency between the author's actions and his declarations ... it may be said ... he was not sure the money would be applied as he thinks it ought to be, by the present ministers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether an author's political acts match their stated principles; account for apparent inconsistencies and whether justifications are plausible rather than ad hoc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid claiming credit for measures one did not effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The author, I believe, will not claim any part of the glory of it: he will leave it whole and entire to the authors of the measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check authors' attributions: ensure praise or blame is properly assigned to actual actors and that writers do not appropriate others' achievements for rhetorical advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate taxation proposals in light of credit and institutional purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Such establishments are our great moneyed companies. To tax them would be critical and dangerous, and contradictory to the very purpose of their institution; which is credit, and cannot therefore be taxation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing taxes on institutions whose function is credit (e.g., banks, chartered companies), consider the adverse effect on the institution's purpose and on national credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't remove a necessary revenue before its replacement is secured
rubrics_metrics.description: What! to take off a revenue so necessary to our being, before anything whatsoever was acquired in the place of it? In prudence, he ought to have waited at least for the first quarter's receipt of the new anonymous American revenue, and Irish land-tax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require that revenue reductions be timed only after replacement income is certain and actually flowing; avoid preemptive relief that leaves a fiscal gap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be precise rather than nugatory when invoking tradition or law
rubrics_metrics.description: If he means, that the particular law, 12 Car. II. c. 19 ... is to be adhered to, and that the several subsequent additions, amendments, and exceptions, ought to be all repealed? If so, he will make a strange havoc ... If he does not mean this, he has got no farther than a nugatory proposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand precision when an author appeals to historical laws or traditions; vague references to 'adherence' are either radical (and must be spelled out) or trivial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess complexity claims about regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: That 'the regulations for the colony trade would be few and simple if the old navigation laws were adhered to,' I utterly deny as a fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenge assertions that complex regulatory systems can be made 'few and simple' without concrete explanation; evaluate the inherent complexity of the subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh the balance between rights/power and prudence
rubrics_metrics.description: It is easy to parade with a high talk of Parliamentary rights, of the universality of legislative powers ... they must see the object to be of proper magnitude to engage them;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate legal/constitutional authority ('we may') from prudential advisability ('we ought'): just because a power exists does not mean exercising it is wise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine whether proposals unduly jeopardize trade, navigation, and manufactures
rubrics_metrics.description: By this manoeuvre, he left our trade, navigation, and manufactures, on the verge of destruction, our finances in ruin, our credit expiring ... All this for want of 300,000_l._
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess downstream economic impacts of fiscal or regulatory measures on trade, navigation, and domestic industry; small-sounding changes can produce outsized damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide concrete schemes not mere speculation
rubrics_metrics.description: He cannot doubt that the present ministry are as well inclined to drive them by their mock inquiries, and real rescinding bills, as he can possibly be with his taxes ... So much for these revenues; which are nothing but his visions, or already the national possessions without any act of his.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require concrete operational plans (how taxes will be levied, administered, collected) instead of speculative lists of possible revenue sources or abstract numerical claims.
